extracted.intended_audience: general readers, citizens, political activists, abolitionists
extracted.subtask_description: An extended 19th-century political-ethical essay arguing when and how individuals should refuse allegiance to unjust government and act from conscience rather than law. It lays out moral criteria and practical measures for nonviolent resistance (tax refusal, resignation, imprisonment) against slavery and unjust war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience over law
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizen must not resign his conscience to the legislator; 'The only obligation which I have a right to assume, is to do at any time what I think right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau argues repeatedly that one should 'be men first, and subjects afterward.' Respect should be for right rather than mere law; law 'never made men a whit more just.' This criterion rejects blind legalism and prioritizes individual moral judgment over statutory obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break laws that make you the agent of injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a law 'is of such a nature that it requires you to be the agent of injustice to another, then, I say, break the law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active noncompliance when compliance would make you complicit (examples: slavery, war). 'Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine.' The essay contrasts tolerable 'friction' with institutionalized mechanisms whose sole function is oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of revolution when tyranny or inefficiency are great and unendurable
rubrics_metrics.description: All men recognize the right of revolution — the right to refuse allegiance and resist government 'when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau locates legitimate civil disobedience in circumstances of organized oppression (he cites slavery and the Mexican war). He rejects waiting for a majority as the only legitimate remedy when justice demands immediate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action from principle, not mere opinion or voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Action from principle — the perception and the performance of right — 'changes things and relations' and is essentially revolutionary; mere opinion or voting is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting is described as 'a sort of gaming' that often amounts to doing nothing effective. True moral action requires acting on principle (including accepting penalties), not merely expressing agreement or casting a vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdraw support (personally and financially) from unjust government
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who oppose injustice should 'effectually withdraw their support, both in person and property, from the government ... and not wait till they constitute a majority of one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures include refusing to pay taxes, refusing to serve, and otherwise withdrawing cooperation so that the individual is not financing or sustaining the State's unjust acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept imprisonment and penalties as the proper place for a just person
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a government which imprisons unjustly, 'the true place for a just man is also a prison.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau frames jail as an honorable locus of protest where truth can be more powerfully asserted; he recounts his own night in jail as clarifying and freeing. Imprisonment is both sacrifice and effective witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the State's slow/legal remedies when they perpetuate evil
rubrics_metrics.description: The State's provided methods for remedying evil 'take too much time' and sometimes the Constitution itself 'is the evil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau criticizes reliance on petitions, legislation, and slow institutional change (Paley's expediency rule). When institutional remedies preserve injustice or are complicit, individuals should not delay moral action awaiting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: One honest person constitutes a majority of one
rubrics_metrics.description: Any man more right than his neighbors 'constitutes a majority of one already.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral authority does not depend on numbers. Thoreau insists that one individual's principled refusal can have decisive moral force and catalyze broader change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax resistance as a peaceable revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to pay taxes that fund injustice is 'the simplest, the most effectual ... mode of expressing little satisfaction with and love for' the State; 'If a thousand men were not to pay their tax-bills this year ... that would not be a violent and bloody measure, as it would be to pay them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax refusal is proposed as a practical, nonviolent measure to deprive the State of means to commit violence (e.g., war, slavery). Thoreau frames it as both symbolic and materially consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resign offices rather than act for the State
rubrics_metrics.description: If a public officer truly wishes to do anything, 'resign your office.' When the subject has refused allegiance and the officer has resigned, 'then the revolution is accomplished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual officials who refuse to be instruments of injustice should step down rather than continue to lend legitimacy to the State. Resignation of officers removes the State's ability to act through them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not support unjust institutions indirectly; sever associative obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: One should refuse to be regarded as a member of incorporated societies one has not joined and decline indirect support for institutions (Thoreau refused to be taxed for a minister he did not attend).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include declaring non-membership and refusing contributions enforced by the State. This criterion emphasizes severing both direct and indirect ties that make one complicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's authority is physical force, not moral persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The State 'never intentionally confronts a man's sense, intellectual or moral, but only his body, his senses' — it is armed with superior physical strength, not superior wit or honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of legal coercion: while the State can punish bodies, it cannot compel conscience. This underpins nonviolent resistance strategies that accept bodily penalties while preserving moral autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure justice beyond expediency; sometimes justice must be done 'cost what it may'
rubrics_metrics.description: Paley's rule of resolving civil obligation into expediency is inadequate; there are cases 'to which the rule of expediency does not apply, in which a people, as well as an individual, must do justice, cost what it may.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral calculus rather than prudential cost–benefit when rights of persons are at stake (Thoreau's example: return the plank to the drowning man even if you drown). This justifies radical action even at great personal or collective expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an active minority rather than a passive majority-conformer
rubrics_metrics.description: A minority that 'clogs by its whole weight' is irresistible; a minority is powerless while it conforms to the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau urges concentrated, principled noncompliance (full withdrawal of cooperation), not token gestures or half-measures. The effectiveness comes from committed, visible resistance rather than passive agreement with majority norms.
